tldr: By expanding a walking style prior distilled from human motion capture data via multi-task reinforcement learning, natural whole-body coordination, high tracking accuracy, and robust steering control are achieved with a single lightweight MLP.
hero_caption: Demonstration results of embodied locomotion intelligence on hardware using HuMBLE. It achieves a public live demonstration on the Boston Dynamics Atlas R1 (A), continuous speed and turning steering (B), Atlas D1 backward walking, turning, and sidestepping (C), smooth gait transitions from walking to sprinting on the Unitree G1 (D), and hierarchical integration with high-level navigation and parkour control (E).
overview:
In humanoid locomotion control, balancing natural, smooth human-like movement with agile, robust tracking across a wide range of velocity commands has long been a difficult challenge. Optimizing purely for task tracking using reinforcement learning (RL) tends to produce mechanical, stiff gaits. Conversely, directly mimicking human motion capture data suffers from out-of-distribution issues, where the robot falls or becomes unresponsive when given commands outside the data distribution, such as unobserved speeds or sharp turns.

To address this, the authors propose "HuMBLE," a learning framework that decouples style acquisition and command space expansion into two stages. In the first stage, a Teacher policy trained to track full-body reference trajectories is distilled into a Student policy (Prior policy) conditioned solely on proprioception and planar velocity commands. In the subsequent second stage, this Prior policy is fine-tuned using multi-task RL, splitting parallel environments equally between a short-horizon reference-guided tracking task and a long-horizon arbitrary velocity-tracking task. This preserves the human locomotion style as a regularizer while robustly adapting to velocity ranges beyond the dataset.

Validation was conducted not only in simulation but also on three completely different humanoid robot hardware platforms: Boston Dynamics Atlas R1, Atlas D1, and Unitree G1. As a result, while maintaining biomimetic characteristics such as synchronized arm swinging, knee extension, and heel-strike to toe roll-off, the policy achieved command-tracking accuracy and disturbance rejection comparable to a Tabula Rasa RL baseline trained without human data (withstanding pushes up to 1400 N on the Atlas R1). The inference time is extremely lightweight at just 1.1 ms on a Jetson Orin CPU, successfully enabling real-world joystick control and integration into hierarchical control stacks.
contributions: Curation and release of a humanoid motion dataset covering approximately 3 hours and 520k frames of locomotion across diverse speeds and omnidirectional trajectories
Proposal of a two-stage learning framework that decouples style acquisition (Teacher-Student distillation) and command space expansion (multi-task RL) to balance naturalness and steerability

Development of training stabilization techniques, including Goal-Conditioned Reference State Initialization (GC-RSI) starting rollouts near target velocities, and a Critic design conditioned on task context
Zero-shot demonstration of high-quality, robust steering locomotion across three distinct humanoid robots: Atlas R1, Atlas D1, and Unitree G1

sections.heading: Why is it hard to combine human-like walking with steerability?
sections.summary: Human-like walking provides predictability and approachable interactions, but conventional model predictive control and task-focused RL tend to produce mechanical movements. Meanwhile, data-driven imitation methods struggle with out-of-distribution commands, leading HuMBLE to clearly separate style learning from command space expansion.
sections.details:
For robots collaborating with humans, locomotion serves as a critical visual and social signal, helping people anticipate subsequent actions and fostering trust. However, achieving human-like locomotion on physical humanoid robots faces a fundamental trade-off.

Traditional Model Predictive Control (MPC) and task-rewarded Reinforcement Learning (RL) excel at command tracking and recovery from falls. Yet, mathematically formalizing delicate whole-body coordination—such as arm swings, gait phases, and heel-to-toe roll-off—is notoriously difficult, often resulting in awkward, mechanical gaits. On the other hand, approaches using human motion capture data, such as Adversarial Motion Priors (AMP) and deep generative models (Diffusion, Flow-Matching), can produce natural behaviors. However, they suffer from min-max training instabilities and computational limits that prevent real-time, low-latency deployment on robot onboard computers. Furthermore, these methods tend to break down when given sharp turns or diagonal movements that do not exist in the training data.

To overcome these issues, HuMBLE formulates locomotion as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP). The framework adopts a two-stage pipeline: first acquiring a motion style prior through Teacher-Student distillation using full-body reference poses as privileged information during training, and then expanding the command range via fine-tuning without corrupting the style. At execution time, this yields an extremely lightweight control policy that requires no generative sampling or reference trajectory inputs, computing joint target angles directly from proprioception and planar velocity commands.

sections.heading: The HuMBLE framework: from distillation to multi-task fine-tuning
sections.summary: After retargeting human motion data to robots and annotating command labels, HuMBLE trains policies in two stages: learning a prior policy via Teacher-Student distillation (Stage I), and expanding command coverage while preserving style using multi-task RL (Stage II).
sections.details:
### Dataset Collection and Command Annotation
Using a Vicon motion capture system, approximately 3 hours (528,214 frames) of human walking data were recorded. This was retargeted to robot kinematic skeletons via two-stage spatio-temporal optimization to avoid self-collisions and ground penetrations. Each frame was annotated with planar velocity commands (longitudinal $v_{\text{long}}$, lateral $v_{\text{lat}}$, and turning yaw rate $\omega_{\text{turn}}$ as $SE(2)$ commands) estimated from torso linear and angular velocities while accounting for future movement intent. To ensure bilateral symmetry, sagittal plane data reflection augmentation was also applied.

### Policy Input-Output Architecture
The final deployment policy $\pi_{\text{deploy}}$ is a simple, fully connected Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Inputs consist solely of the robot's proprioception $\bm{o}_{\text{prop}}$ (IMU linear and angular velocities, projected gravity vector, joint positions, joint velocities, and previous action) and the user command $\bm{o}_{\text{cmd}}$, running inference at 50 Hz. The outputs are target joint position offsets for low-level PD controllers.

### Stage I: Prior Policy Acquisition via Distillation
A Teacher policy $\pi_{\text{teacher}}$, which directly observes full-body reference joint poses $\bm{o}_{\text{ref}}$, is trained via PPO (Asymmetric Actor-Critic) to track reference trajectories. Next, using DAgger-style distillation, a Student policy $\pi_{\text{prior}}$ that observes only $\bm{o}_{\text{deploy}}$ without reference trajectories is trained to imitate the Teacher's actions. This acquires a motion prior that reconstructs natural whole-body coordinated movements even under partial observability.

### Stage II: Command Expansion via Multi-Task RL
Directly fine-tuning the Prior policy on arbitrary commands causes style collapse. To prevent this, multi-task RL is introduced, splitting parallel simulation environments into two sets:
- Short-horizon reference-guided tracking task ($\mathbb{E}_{\text{ref}}$): Tracks dataset reference trajectories for short horizons, acting as an explicit regularizer to retain human-like style.
- Long-horizon goal-conditioned task ($\mathbb{E}_{\text{goal}}$): Tracks randomly sampled arbitrary velocity commands over long horizons, boosting responsiveness and robustness to out-of-distribution commands.

In addition, "Goal-Conditioned Reference State Initialization (GC-RSI)" starts episodes from states matching the target command to prevent falls, while supplying the Critic with a task indicator flag $o_{\text{sup}} \in \{0, 1\}$ allows stable evaluation across the two distinct reward functions.

captions.F6: Overall HuMBLE framework. In Stage I, a Teacher policy observing full-body reference trajectories is distilled into a Prior policy conditioned only on proprioception and SE(2) commands. In Stage II, multi-task RL pairing short-horizon reference tracking and long-horizon goal tracking achieves command expansion while preserving motion style.

sections.heading: Experimental results: How agile can it be while staying natural?
sections.summary: HuMBLE accurately reproduces human-specific walking styles such as arm swinging and heel-to-toe roll-off, while matching data-free RL baselines in command tracking accuracy and disturbance rejection. Hardware experiments also confirm minimal transfer error from simulation.
sections.details:
### Qualitative Gait Feature Comparisons
On the Atlas R1, HuMBLE was compared against Boston Dynamics' standard MPC and a Tabula Rasa RL policy trained without human data. While the MPC exhibited stiff, fixed arms and Tabula Rasa RL adopted unnatural postures, HuMBLE displayed synchronized arm swinging, knee locking at ground contact, and distinct heel-strike to toe roll-off. Smooth transitions from low-speed shuffling to dynamic high-speed walking also emerged automatically.

### Motion Data Fidelity (Quantitative Evaluation)
On the Unitree G1, Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) alignment errors against reference motions were evaluated. The mean absolute errors (MAE) of the deployed HuMBLE policy were 0.058 m/s for torso linear velocity, 0.127 rad/s for angular velocity, and 0.055 rad for joint positions—corresponding to just 0.149, 0.257, and 0.184 times the dataset standard deviations, respectively. This confirms that whole-body motion can be reconstructed at a level close to the privileged Teacher policy.

### Tracking Accuracy, Responsiveness, and Robustness
Evaluating step responses across the planar velocity space revealed that HuMBLE's steady-state tracking error is nearly identical to Tabula Rasa RL. For small velocity commands near zero, tracking accuracy exceeded the baseline thanks to shuffling motions present in the dataset. Furthermore, in push tests applying 0.2-second perturbation forces to the Atlas R1 torso, the robot withstood impacts up to 1400 N in dominant directions. Gait-dependent stability characteristics naturally appeared, showing stronger resistance forward and backward during forward walking, and lateral resistance during sidestepping.

### Sim-to-Real Transfer and Real-World Applications
Across all three robot platforms, differences in tracking error between hardware and simulation remained within 0.05 m/s for linear velocity and 0.10 rad/s for angular velocity, demonstrating high transfer fidelity. Inference time on the Unitree G1 onboard Jetson AGX Orin CPU was only 1.1 ms. Beyond indoor and outdoor joystick teleoperation, the policy operated seamlessly as a low-level module for obstacle-avoidance navigation and box-climbing parkour control.

sections.heading: Ablation studies: Why was this two-stage design necessary?
sections.summary: Ablations reveal that single-stage imitation fails at complex whole-body coordination like sidestepping, and that the ratio of parallel environments in Stage II forms a clear Pareto trade-off between style preservation and command-tracking performance.
sections.details:
### Necessity of Teacher-Student Distillation
In Stage I, HuMBLE was compared against a single-stage baseline that performed imitation learning directly in the partially observable space without an intermediate Teacher. While the baseline handled simple forward walking to some degree, tracking errors worsened by up to over 70%. Furthermore, on sidestepping, which demands sophisticated whole-body coordination and lateral balance, the baseline froze in an upright stance after a few steps and failed completely (linear velocity error surged by over 240%). This demonstrates that decoupling physical constraint satisfaction from observation limitation handling across two stages is essential.

### Multi-Task RL Environment Allocation Ratio
In Stage II, the allocation ratio between the reference-guided environment (Ref) and goal-tracking environment (Goal) was varied from 0:100 to 100:0.
- Goal 100% (0:100): Command tracking error reached its minimum, but unnatural torso oscillations and degraded arm swing immediately destroyed human-likeness.
- Ref 100% (100:0): Motion fidelity was highest, but the robot fell when issued lateral commands sparsely represented in the dataset.

This ratio forms a distinct Pareto trade-off curve between style fidelity and tracking accuracy, showing that the 50:50 ratio chosen in this work provides the optimal operating point for adapting to unseen commands without breaking human-like gait patterns.

(B) Varying the allocation ratio between Ref and Goal environments reveals a clear trade-off curve between motion style fidelity and velocity tracking error.

sections.heading: Discussion and future outlook: Toward general-purpose embodied AI
sections.summary: HuMBLE combines human-like movement with practical robustness using a single lightweight MLP by decoupling style learning from command expansion. While currently limited to flat-ground walking, it holds promise for whole-body loco-manipulation and teleoperation.
sections.details:
The key achievement of HuMBLE is resolving the tension between natural human-likeness and agile, robust command tracking within a clean, interpretable reinforcement learning framework. Accomplishing this with a single small MLP—without latent space sampling or heavy generative models—provides a massive practical advantage for onboard deployment.

Nevertheless, the current framework faces several limitations:
- Restriction to Flat Ground: The system is currently specialized for flat terrain. Navigating stairs or leaping over obstacles requires exteroceptive perception (cameras, LiDAR) and corresponding new motion datasets.
- Annotation Scalability: While planar velocity command labels were automatically computed via finite differences, scaling to abstract semantics like natural language instructions increases labeling complexity.
- Policy Capacity Bounds: Although 3 hours of walking data fit into a single MLP, whether the same compact architecture can scale to broader, higher-dimensional repertoires—such as loco-manipulation or dynamic teleoperation—remains an open question for future work.

Even so, the HuMBLE recipe of distilling a prior from motion data and expanding its command space via multi-task RL serves as a general-purpose methodology applicable across embodied intelligence beyond locomotion.

takeaways: Decoupling motion imitation (style acquisition) from command tracking (out-of-distribution expansion) into Teacher-Student distillation and multi-task RL is highly effective.
Splitting parallel simulation environments 50:50 between reference tracking and task tracking serves as an effective regularizer to prevent style collapse.
A single lightweight MLP (inference time ~1 ms) can express full-body coordination and deploy directly to hardware without generative models or latent variables.
Goal-Conditioned Reference State Initialization (GC-RSI) matching target commands and providing task indicator flags to the Critic are essential keys to stabilizing multi-task RL training.
limitations: Locomotion is limited to flat ground, and integrating exteroceptive sensing (cameras, LiDAR) for walking on uneven terrain or stairs remains unverified.
Per-frame command annotations rely on torso velocity differences, requiring additional techniques to extend to higher-level modalities such as language instructions.
The capacity limits of a single small MLP when scaling to larger, more diverse datasets (e.g., whole-body manipulation or martial arts) remain unknown.
